The impact spans 15,000 users and a 45‑minute outage, suggesting the issue is not trivial but also not deeply entangled across multiple services. The root cause is likely a single component (Redis) hitting its memory limit, requiring capacity planning or eviction policy changes. Therefore, the failure is categorized as storage_exhaustion with a moderate level of operational complexity.

output.security_notes: Verify write freeze before node reboot. Promote read-replica prior to primary teardown.

recurring_patterns.symptom_pattern: Redis memory usage > 98% with maxmemory-policy noeviction

diagnostic_stage_assessment.notes: Current telemetry aligns with historical storage_exhaustion incidents (e.g., INC-1005). While the service differs, the underlying resource exhaustion pattern recurs, suggesting a likely root cause related to Redis memory limits.

output.governing_sla_rule: Tier-1 service impacting >= 500 users, or cross-tier impact >= 2,000 users.
output.justification: The incident impacts 15,000 users, far exceeding the cross‑tier threshold of 2,000 users defined in the SLA rule. Although the affected service is Tier‑2, the rule applies when the aggregate user impact across tiers surpasses 2,000, triggering at least SEV‑2. The outage duration of 45 minutes is within the response window for SEV‑2 (typically <1 hour) and does not warrant escalation to SEV‑1, which is reserved for Tier‑1 services affecting >=500 users or critical business‑impacting failures. Therefore, the deterministic rule and the telemetry justify confirming the final severity as SEV‑2.

remediation_steps.title: Validate Operator Access and Cluster Context
remediation_steps.description: Ensure the operator has the required ProdOperations role and that kubectl is pointed at the production EKS cluster.
verification: AWS identity ARN matches ProdOperations role
kubectl context name contains 'prod'
Node list returns expected production worker nodes

remediation_steps.title: Confirm Redis Memory Exhaustion and Identify Hot Keys
remediation_steps.description: Collect real‑time memory metrics from the Redis primary and enumerate keys consuming the most memory.
commands: kubectl exec -n cache redis-primary-0 -- redis-cli INFO memory
kubectl exec -n cache redis-primary-0 -- redis-cli --scan | while read key; do echo "$key $(kubectl exec -n cache redis-primary-0 -- redis-cli MEMORY USAGE $key)"; done | sort -k2 -n -r | head -20
verification: "used_memory" > 98% of "maxmemory"
Top 20 keys account for > 60% of used memory

remediation_steps.title: Apply Write‑Freeze and Promote Read‑Replica to Primary
remediation_steps.description: Prevent further writes to the exhausted primary, promote the healthy read‑replica, and point the service to the new primary.
commands: kubectl exec -n cache redis-replica-0 -- redis-cli -p 6379 REPLICAOF NO ONE
# Update Service Endpoint (if using a ConfigMap)
kubectl patch configmap inventory-api-config -n prod --type merge -p '{"data":{"REDIS_HOST":"redis-replica-0.cache.svc.cluster.local"}}'
verification: Write‑freeze endpoint returns status 200
Replica reports role "master" in INFO replication
ConfigMap reflects new REDIS_HOST value

remediation_steps.title: Increase Redis Maxmemory Limit and Adjust Eviction Policy
remediation_steps.description: Raise the maxmemory setting to accommodate current load and switch to an eviction policy that safely discards least‑recently‑used keys.
commands: # In the container args, add or modify:
verification: After pod restart, `redis-cli CONFIG GET maxmemory` returns >= 4gb
`redis-cli CONFIG GET maxmemory-policy` returns "allkeys-lru"
Memory usage stabilises below 80% of maxmemory within 5 minutes

remediation_steps.title: Perform Graceful Rolling Restart of Inventory‑API Pods
remediation_steps.description: Refresh the API pods so they reconnect to the newly promoted Redis primary and pick up the updated configuration.
verification: All inventory‑api pods report READY=1/1 and STATUS=Running
Health endpoint returns HTTP 200
Application logs no longer contain ERR_STORAGE_EXHAUSTION_333

rollback_plan.overall_strategy: Revert Redis configuration and primary/replica roles to their pre‑remediation state, and undo the inventory‑api deployment rollout if service health degrades.

steps.description: Disable write‑freeze to allow normal write traffic.
verification: Write‑freeze endpoint returns status 200 and confirms disabled

steps.description: Demote the promoted replica back to read‑only and re‑promote the original primary.
commands: kubectl exec -n cache redis-replica-0 -- redis-cli REPLICAOF $(kubectl get svc redis-primary -n cache -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIP}') 6379
kubectl exec -n cache redis-primary-0 -- redis-cli REPLICAOF NO ONE
verification: Original primary reports role "master" in INFO replication
Former replica reports role "slave"

steps.description: Restore original Redis maxmemory and eviction policy.
commands: # Revert args to previous values, e.g., --maxmemory 2gb --maxmemory-policy noeviction
verification: `redis-cli CONFIG GET maxmemory` matches pre‑remediation value
`redis-cli CONFIG GET maxmemory-policy` matches pre‑remediation value

steps.description: Undo inventory‑api deployment to previous image tag.
verification: Pods run the prior container image (verify via `kubectl get pod -l app=inventory-api -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.containers[0].image}'`)
Health endpoint returns HTTP 200

prerequisite_checks: Operator credentials verified for ProdOperations role
Current Redis configuration snapshot saved (kubectl get configmap/statefulset yaml > backup)
Rollback procedures reviewed and approved by change management
